title: CompareBench: Quality Monitoring & A/B Scenario Walkthrough - Orion Analytics
summary: Redwood demo focused on CompareBench and regression alerts. Walkthrough of prompt sets, A/B comparisons, noise handling, and runbook for rolling back models. Customer cares about PO C metrics, SLOs, and how alerts tie to product telemetry. Next steps: pilot access, pricing estimate, run a small A/B with 5k requests and provide checklist for SOC2 QA.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood here. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Lena: Hi, I'm Lena, Director of ML at Orion. Marcus and Priya are with me.
[00:12] Marcus: Hey all.
[00:14] Priya: Hi — thanks for setting this up.
[00:17] Maya: Great. Ethan, want to intro?
[00:20] Ethan: Yeah, hey team. I'm Ethan, SE on the observability and Optimize side. Today we want to run through our CompareBench tooling — prompt set-driven monitoring, regression alerts, and A/B compare flow.
[00:31] Priya: Perfect, we built a couple of prompt families yesterday to test, so this should be useful.
[00:36] Ethan: Awesome. I'll share my screen — apologies if the demo is a little grainy.
[00:44] [screen share starts]
[01:05] Ethan: Okay on the console you can see 'CompareBench' — we load prompt sets, attach expected outputs or quality labels, and run up evals either offline or as streaming checks.
[01:20] Marcus: Quick question, can this compare across model variants and quantized builds?
[01:24] Ethan: Yes — we route by model id, version and also tag quantization profiles. The compare engine normalizes tokenization diffs, but you'll see minor noise sometimes — like tokenization causing small diffs, we show a diff heatmap.
[01:40] Lena: How do you define regressed vs noisy? Our throughput has a lot of paraphrase variance.
[01:47] Ethan: Good call. There are a couple of levers: threshold-based alerts on metric deltas, per-prompt tolerances, and a noise-robust metric they call 'consensus F1' which aggregates human-labeled acceptance. You can also attach a qualification prompt set to ignore high-variance prompts.
[02:10] Marcus: So if we see 5% drop in semantic-similarity across the board, that's an automatic alert?
[02:16] Ethan: Depends on your rule. Default SLO is a 3% absolute drop on mean similarity with a two-sided p-value check and sample size gating. We can demo A/B to show significance.
[02:29] [05:12] Ethan: Switching to live A/B: I've got model A (open-llama-13b-8k) and model B (quantized 8-bit variant). We push a 1k sample prompt set to both, and the UI surfaces per-prompt pass/fail and an aggregate.
[05:35] Priya: Can we import our telemetry keys? We'd like to correlate customer-facing errors in our product with these regressions.
[05:42] Ethan: Yeah — we have connectors for DataDog, Segment, and an event webhook. You can map request_id to your session id to link traces.
[05:50] Marcus: Any gotchas with KV cache or streaming inference? We have a lot of long-convo contexts.
[05:58] Ethan: Good point. Our runtime exposes sequence-length buckets. For long contexts the effective latency distribution shifts and we tag evals by context length. Also note sometimes transcripts auto-gen 'KV cash' — internal joke, but seriously watch for KV cache priming effects in your prompts.
[06:18] [07:02] Maya: To jump in — typical pilot we recommend 5k total evals across your high-impact prompt families, run A/B for one week with traffic split, and then use rollout policies tied to regression alerts.
[07:18] Lena: What's the false positive rate like? We can't have noisy alerts every day.
[07:22] Ethan: You can tune alert windows and require multiple signal types — e.g., similarity drop + increased rejection rate + product error spike. We also provide a 'learning mute' that suppresses alerts on known high-variance prompts for 48 hours during model changes.
[07:40] Marcus: Walk me through the runbook if an alert fires.
[07:44] Ethan: Sure, in the console there's a Runbook template: triage steps, sample-size check, quick A/B rollback, and canary/traffic-split for verification. The runbook includes suggested commands for the CLI and links to the Dedicated rollback API.
[07:58] Priya: Is the runbook editable? We want to add our internal incident playbook.
[08:02] Ethan: Yep, you can clone and edit, and attach Slack runbook triggers.
[08:08] [09:15] Lena: Security — does CompareBench see raw PII when we run evals on customer data? We have strict requirements.
[09:21] Maya: We recommend redacting or hashing PII before sending. For Private deployments we can run the whole stack in your VPC and configure KMS.
[09:30] Marcus: If we use Hosted, is data persisted?
[09:33] Ethan: By default eval artifacts are retained 30 days with options for extended retention as an add-on; we can also configure no-persist for certain prompt sets. All storage encrypted at rest.
[09:45] [11:06] Maya: Let's demo an alert setup — Ethan set a threshold across mean semantic similarity and a second rule on hallucination-rate per prompt family.
[11:12] Ethan: Adding alert: metric=semantic_similarity, comparator=relative_drop, threshold=0.03, window=6h, min_samples=200. Second rule: hallucination_rate>0.05 for more than 3 consecutive windows. Combine with AND.
[11:34] Marcus: Cool. How do you measure hallucination rate automatically?
[11:38] Ethan: We use a hybrid approach — classifier-based detection plus human-in-the-loop annotations from your label set. For pilot we suggest seeding 500 hand-labeled prompts to calibrate.
[11:50] [13:45] Priya: Can alerts be routed to on-call? We use PagerDuty.
[13:49] Ethan: Yes, webhook, PagerDuty, and email. You can create per-route escalation policies.
[14:05] Lena: Show the A/B significance test.
[14:08] Ethan: Running the test now — it computes a bootstrap confidence interval on mean similarity and a delta for the aggregation. You can pick metrics: ROUGE, BLEU, embedding-sim, consensus F1. Here's the chart — model B has a -2.4% delta, but 95% CI includes zero, p=0.12 so not significant.
[14:34] Marcus: Hmm — sample size seems low.
[14:36] Ethan: Correct — UI shows recommended sample to reach 80% power based on observed variance.
[14:45] [17:20] Maya: A common ask is "how to tie grading rubric to product-level SLOs" — Ethan?
[17:25] Ethan: You define a mapping: prompt-family labels map to product intents; then set composite metrics. For example if you care most about intent classification accuracy, make that first-class metric and weight alerts towards it.
[17:40] Lena: How do we handle multi-turn where context influences label?
[17:44] Ethan: We provide conversation anchors and can snapshot the KV state; evals can be run on conversation prefixes to emulate production behavior. There will be more noise so we recommend larger sample sizes and higher tolerances.
[17:58] [20:01] Marcus: Integration: do we need to change request payloads?
[20:04] Ethan: Minimal changes: include a meta field with session_id and prompt_family tag; for streaming you can optionally send end-of-turn markers.
[20:12] Priya: On pilot UX — can product managers see the dashboard without full infra access?
[20:16] Maya: Yes, RBAC is per-dashboard role; read-only viewers are common.
[20:21] [23:00] Ethan: Now showing anomaly view — heatmaps over time. You can drill to examples, copy failed prompts to a 'quarantine set' for labelers, or push to a 'retrain bucket'.
[23:14] Lena: Does quarantine integrate with our annotation tool? We use LabelForge — any connector?
[23:18] Ethan: We don't have LabelForge out of the box but we can export CSV or hook a webhook. Connector request noted.
[23:25] Marcus: Let's talk about cost: running 5k evals a week — what's the estimate?
[23:30] Maya: Rough ballpark depends on models. For a 13B on hosted with batching optimizations, maybe $X per 1k tokens — then Optimize suggests caching and batching to cut unit cost by up to 40%. We'll send a pricing worksheet.
[23:48] Priya: Would dedicated help with predictable SLOs?
[23:52] Ethan: Dedicated gives reserved capacity and stronger tail latency SLAs. For high-throughput evals it's recommended.
[24:00] [27:10] Maya: Quick objection handling — customers worry about too many false regressions, but the combination of per-prompt tolerances, multi-signal alerts, and mute windows reduces noise materially.
[27:25] Marcus: For the pilot, what's the success criteria?
[27:29] Maya: We'd propose 1) detect a regression that would have been missed by your current monitoring, or 2) reduce mean error rate by X% after a rollout, or 3) demonstrate integration mapping to product SLOs.
[27:45] Lena: Timeline for pilot?
[27:48] Maya: We generally run a 4-week pilot after initial 2-week setup. 1 week for ingest and labeling, 2 weeks for A/B, 1 week for analysis.
[27:58] Priya: Any legal or security paperwork?
[28:02] Maya: We'll share SOC2 docs and a data processing addendum. For Private, we can offer on-prem.
[28:10] [30:00] Ethan: Opening the API: you can run evaluations via the Redwood API — snippet: POST /v1/evals with prompt_set_id, model_id, and expected_label. Response includes per-example score, tokens, and model_latency.
[30:18] Marcus: Is there a quota/burst limit for evals?
[30:21] Ethan: Yes on hosted there are rate limits but pilot customers often get elevated quotas. For Dedicated you control throughput.
[30:30] [34:12] Maya: Let's surface the replay feature — if you detect a regression you can replay traffic against older model versions to confirm. This is handy for intermittent regressions.
[34:25] Priya: Can replay use live user data or only anonymized sets?
[34:29] Ethan: Both — but for live we recommend token redaction and privacy hooks.
[34:40] Lena: Any SDK support for our python stack?
[34:44] Ethan: Yep python, node and a CLI. We'll include a sample notebook for the pilot.
[34:55] [38:02] Marcus: How do alerts show in the console for multi-model rollouts?
[38:06] Ethan: You can filter by model tag, version, or rollout ID. For gradual rollouts we show a small-multiplicity view with cohort metrics.
[38:18] Priya: Do you support tagging experiments with Jira IDs?
[38:21] Ethan: Yes, metadata fields allowed. We can auto-create Jira tickets on critical alerts.
[38:30] [41:00] Maya: Recap: pilot scope, success criteria, pricing doc, SOC2 and DPA, sample notebook.
[41:08] Lena: Sounds good. Marcus any final tech concerns?
[41:11] Marcus: One more — inference determinism across quantized builds. Sometimes a 1-bit change flips outputs.
[41:17] Ethan: We surface a bit-flip sensitivity analysis — run a small sweep and report instability rate; we can also bias rollouts away from unstable quota profiles.
[41:30] Priya: Great — let's put dates.
[41:34] Maya: I'll propose a pilot start next Monday, Jan 19.
[41:39] Lena: That works for us.
[41:42] [46:00] Maya: Ok final logistics — we'll send the pilot checklist, include team access, and attach the pricing sheet.
[46:10] Priya: Appreciate it. One ask: can the alert UI bulk mute by prompt tag?
[46:15] Ethan: Yes, we have bulk mute and 'snooze by tag' UI.
[46:22] Marcus: OK thanks everyone.
[46:25] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the docs and invite for kickoff.
[46:30] [call ends]
